# 242,072 malware flags on npm and PyPI, and what the registries did about them

#security #opensource #npm #python

Security feeds publish lists of malicious packages, and dependency scanners turn those lists into
red alerts in your CI. How often is a flag right? Nobody publishes that number per feed, so we
started measuring it, with the method written down and committed before we looked at a single
result. We also ran four open-source scanners on known malware and on a week of new uploads, to see
what a flag costs at a registry's real volume. For completeness of the analysis, we also measured
what each feed's records show and how each feed answers the people who dispute them.

Our interest, first. One of the feeds below listed nine of our own PyPI packages as malware; it has since reviewed all
nine, withdrawing one and reclassifying eight as vulnerabilities. That is why we looked. They are counted like every other row, each feed gets its numbers a week before
this post, and their answers are part of it. The last section shows how every tool treated our own
packages, labelled for what it is: one interested publisher's case, not a measure of accuracy.

## What we measured

Two open sources, npm and PyPI only:

  * OpenSSF `malicious-packages`: 234,710 records, each naming the tools that reported it. Nine tools have attributable data: Amazon Inspector, ReversingLabs, Checkmarx, OSSF Package Analysis, Google Open Source Security, GitHub's malware advisories, kam193, Oracle Macaron, and Vulnetix (7,362 malware records in its GCVE advisory database). Vulnetix points out that this database is not its malware feed: it went public on 18 October and was still being loaded in bulk when we took our snapshot on the 24th. Its malware feed proper is a set of STIX indicator bundles, which we did not measure here.
  * For a random sample of 7,483 records (up to 400 per tool, ecosystem and kind), we asked npm and PyPI what they serve today. Metadata only: nothing was downloaded or run.

"Registry acted" means the package is gone, replaced by npm's `0.0.1-security` placeholder,
quarantined, or the flagged versions are no longer served. That is a registry agreeing, not proof:
registries act on these same feeds' reports. And a package still up is not proof of a false
positive: registries are slow and miss things. This stage gives no false-positive rate. The next one
does.

## What every tool said about our own packages

We publish 77 packages (52 on PyPI, 25 on npm). Here is what each tool says about them. One
publisher is a case, not a sample; read it as what a maintainer runs into.

  * Eight of the nine feeds (Amazon Inspector, ReversingLabs, Checkmarx, OSSF Package Analysis, Google, GitHub, kam193, Oracle Macaron): nothing. None of the 77 is in their records.
  * Vulnetix: nine PyPI packages listed as malware, June to October. Every matched line we traced is a test, an example or a constant: a test asserting our fetch tool refuses `file:///etc/passwd`, `curl` examples in READMEs, Circle's USDC contract address, the secp256k1 curve order, a cron line in install instructions, `key_path: ~/.ssh/id_rsa` in a configuration guide, and the list of persistence locations our own sandbox watches when it runs other people's packages. We disputed six in their repository on 21 October; three more were found while writing this. Vulnetix reviewed all nine by hand within days: one record withdrawn, eight reclassified from malware to vulnerabilities. And those eight were real: an MCP server that answered anyone when no key was set, a probe that resolved a name twice so a second answer could point it inside our network, sanctions data read incompletely, a permission that survived a runtime change, among others. We fixed all eight and released the fixes; Vulnetix checked the published packages, set the fixed versions on all eight records, and opened five new ones for flaws we described in our own fixes. Thank you, Vulnetix: the review was quick and done in the open, it found real flaws that we have since fixed, and every step of it is public.
  * GuardDog 3.2.0 (open source, DataDog), which we ran ourselves with defaults: no verdict, by design. It lists heuristics for a person to review. Its "threat" heuristics fired on 21 of 86 scans (the latest version of all 77, plus the nine versions Vulnetix flagged, four of which it also questioned): the Telegram API address our hub uses to notify its owner, `.env` and environment reads, WARDEN's own detection patterns for credential paths, `ffmpeg` run with its output silenced, a regular expression for Cyrillic. Each is code doing what it says; a reviewer clears it, and asking for that review is exactly what GuardDog promises.
  * WARDEN, our own MCP firewall, so read this twice as interested: it reads the tool definitions a model sees, not package code, and gives our MCP servers no blocking match. It does attach advisory notes: 12 on our hub's 13 tools, mostly "this tool takes a credential parameter", which is true. 37.5% of all servers in the registry get advisory notes; 1.8% get a blocking match.

The pattern, if one case can show one, is that text rules matching anywhere in a package, tests and
docs included, meet packages that describe attacks: security tools, sandboxes, test suites.
Finding 5 shows how common that is beyond us.

## About

Monthly snapshots of a public transparency log covering remote MCP servers in the official registry and npm and PyPI MCP packages. The files hold the tool definitions each server served, every recorded change field by field, pattern scan matches, and advisory classifier readings. A signed manifest lists checksums so users can verify files, and the data is released under CC BY 4.0.

## What it does

The site says HISTOR reads the tool list of every remote server in the official MCP registry each day and runs each new npm and PyPI MCP package version in a sandbox. It presents its pattern matches and classifier flags as leads worth reading, not as proof that a server is malicious.

### Stated on the product site

License
    CC BY 4.0

Release cadence
    A full snapshot published as files once a month

Verification
    A manifest of file checksums, signed with Ed25519

Mirrors
    Hugging Face with one tag per snapshot, Zenodo with a DOI per snapshot

Coverage limit
    Servers that require a key show less or nothing to the anonymous client

Code link
    The page links a GitHub repository for the project

### Not stated on the site

  * The page does not name the LLM behind the advisory classifier readings.
  * The page does not say what the sandbox run of a package records beyond its tool list.
  * How server operators' opt-out requests are handled beyond opening an issue is not described on the page.

Written from the product site at histor.modelmarket.dev.

## Outside checks

HISTOR is not the only public record of MCP tool definitions. Where another log publishes its reads, the two are compared on the same servers and days, and the result is published both ways, with HISTOR's own misses.

### ScraperWatch

A daily diff of a fixed panel of about 3,000 remote endpoints. HISTOR compares each of their published days with its own reads, and ScraperWatch shows the result on its page under "Outside check". The first comparison found a robots.txt parsing limit on their side and a handshake regression on HISTOR's; both were fixed the same day.

scraperwatch.com/mcp-changes
/datasets/peers/scraperwatch/latest

### heldfast

An open daily record of the tool definitions of the servers in the official MCP registry. Of the 23,190 servers both logs recorded on 26 October 2026, 21,215 had every field in both; on those, 97.9% of servers and 99.1% of tools were identical byte for byte, and each difference has a stated cause: package versions, read times, failed reads, a first page only, an older protocol.

Before your agent trusts a server, send the tools it received. The answer is signed by the log's did:key and names the tree head it was given under.

Image: Two MCP logs matched 23 tools. Five days later, every name had changed.

Compare the latest saved entries for one MCP server and you get zero tool names in common. Compare the observations from the same evening and all 23 tool fingerprints match.

We maintain HISTOR, a transparency log for the tool definitions MCP servers advertise. We wanted to see whether an independent observer could corroborate one of our observations. We picked LEGION-tlog because it publishes a timestamp and a SHA-256 fingerprint for each tool. Those fingerprints let us compare individual definitions even when the logs use different formats for their records. --------------------------------------------------------------------------------
